note: true_positive. WHAT THE EVIDENCE SHOWS: anthropic.provider.ts:3 imports the raw Anthropic SDK and :47 constructs a live client from it, so this is a runtime SDK boundary rather than a type-only reference that a type-import exemption would cover. A tenant credential reaches that client at :56 (chat) and :119 (validateCredential), and :124 issues its own SDK call, so two independent request paths terminate here. The class at :24 injects only a Logger (:26) and a client cache (:27) — nothing at this file's boundary applies rate limiting, token budgeting, content guardrails, audit, or cost attribution. WHY THAT MAKES THE FINDING TRUE: the rule offers two ways to be clean — reach the SDK through the approved wrapper, or be named on the lint-enforced allowlist. The cited file does neither: it IS the raw-import site, and it is not the path the enforcement lists name. WHAT MUST BE DONE: pick one boundary and make the enforcement lists say so. Either name this provider as the designated SDK boundary in both enforcement SSoTs (the ESLint rule's wrapper-path list and the ARIA adapter's built-in allowlist), or route the SDK call back through the wrapper those lists already name. WHY IT MATTERS AND WHAT BREAKS IF SKIPPED: the gate exists so that a second `new Anthropic()` cannot appear unnoticed. When the allowlist names a path that no longer constructs the client, the gate keeps reporting clean while the real boundary is unowned — a Tier-3 'make it detectable' control that has quietly stopped detecting. The next provider file copying this shape inherits the same ungoverned status, and safety-stack coverage at the boundary becomes a convention instead of a structural guarantee. DOWNSTREAM SURFACE: the ai-service agent runtime that serves chat through this provider and the BYOK credential-validation path that calls validateCredential. CORRECT PATH: fix the enforcement SSoT so the named boundary matches the architecture; suppressing the rule, widening it to ignore provider files, or annotating the import would hide the drift rather than close it.

note: FALSE POSITIVE. Anchor is accurate: auth.resolver.ts:141 opens the decorator stack of the refreshToken mutation (@RateLimit at 141, @Public() at 142, @Mutation(() => AuthPayload) at 143), and the rule's mechanical predicate genuinely matches — the adapter is not hallucinating the code shape. The claim fails on its satisfaction condition, not its detection. The rule states the endpoint 'requires an explicit allowlist or tenant-skip rationale', and offers exactly two ways to satisfy it: membership in the caller-supplied path allowlist, or a @SkipTenantGuard() marker. Neither is a real remediation here. (1) The tenant-skip marker is unreachable metadata on a public handler: the platform TenantGuard resolves the public marker first and returns on that branch before it ever reads the skip-tenant key, so stamping @SkipTenantGuard() onto this mutation would change nothing at runtime — it would add dead annotation to satisfy a scanner. The resolver's own structure encodes that convention: every @SkipTenantGuard() use in this file (261, 280, 295, 306) sits on an authenticated non-public operation, and every @Public() operation (112, 142, 169, 208, 233, 255) omits it. (2) The adapter allowlist is keyed on file path, not endpoint, so allowlisting this resolver would suppress every check in the file rather than record a rationale for one mutation. On substance there is no missing boundary. refreshToken must be public — the caller holds no valid access token, which is the entire purpose of refresh. The tenant is resolved server-side from the presented refresh token at line 159; the token is preferentially read from the httpOnly cookie at 151; and the brute-force boundary the rule cares about is present on the anchored line itself (limit 10 per 5 minutes). Contrast this with the real vulnerability class documented in the same file at 89-98: the removed register mutation accepted a client-supplied tenantId with no validation, which is what an ungoverned public write actually looks like. refreshToken has the inverse shape — zero client-supplied tenant input. Rule-health note: the predicate necessarily fires on all five @Public() write mutations in this single file (112, 142, 169, 208, 233), so this is a systematic false-positive class rather than one bad anchor. The root-cause fix is to re-express the rule against the risk it means to catch — a public write that accepts a caller-supplied tenant identifier, or that mutates existing tenant state without a server-resolved credential — instead of testing for a decorator the runtime never reads on this path.

note: WHAT THE FINDING CLAIMS. The rule tests one condition: a route is public, uses a write verb, and declares neither an allowlist registration nor a tenant-skip. WHAT THE EVIDENCE SHOWS. @Public() sits at class level (line 45) and @Post('csp-report') at line 63, so every request to this route reaches the handler without an authenticated principal — that is the precondition, confirmed on decorators, which are behavior, not narration. The file carries no @SkipTenantGuard across its full 99 lines, so the tenant-skip branch of the requirement is unmet in the only channel a gate can read. The header docblock (line 7) and method docblock (lines 53-62) do state why authentication is absent, but a comment is not a declaration: the judge contract bars comments without behavior from discharging a machine-checked requirement, and no scanner, guard, or test consumes that prose. WHAT THE FINDING DOES NOT CLAIM. It does not say this endpoint should require auth. A CSP report-uri must accept credential-less browser POSTs; making it authenticated would make it useless. The defect is that a legitimate exception is undeclared. WHY IT MATTERS AND WHAT BREAKS IF SKIPPED. The gateway's population of unauthenticated write routes is auditable only while every member is registered somewhere a gate reads. Leave one legitimate exception unregistered and the registry stops discriminating: the next @Public() @Post — one that does persist tenant rows — looks identical to this one at scan time, and the reviewer who trusts the registry approves it. That is how a boundary control degrades into decoration. DOWNSTREAM SURFACE. gateway-api's public route boundary, and every later security-boundary scan whose signal depends on the exception set being complete. ROOT-CAUSE REMEDY (tier 3 — make it detectable). Declare the exemption where the machine reads it: add the tenant-skip decorator at the route, or register this path in the adapter allowlist with its reason, so the exemption travels with the code and any future public write route is flagged on merit. CALIBRATION NOTE. Exploitability of this specific route is narrower than the emitted high severity: the handler persists nothing, logging at lines 68-82 and publishing a best-effort security event at line 87. What still argues for an explicitly recorded exemption is line 41 — the body type is open-ended ([key: string]: unknown) and its caller-controlled fields flow into a structured log from an unauthenticated route. Body validation is a separate rule's concern and is not asserted here. CONFIDENCE. Held at 0.84: the tenant-skip branch is fully checkable from the single admissible ref, while the allowlist-registration branch lives in configuration outside the evidence supplied, so that half rests on the absence of any in-file declaration rather than on direct inspection of the registry.
